requirements.requirement: Configure node1 so the kernel boots with audit=1 and the setting persists across reboot.
requirements.summary: The initial running kernel lacked audit=1. The executor added it to the persistent GRUB default and all Linux boot entries, then performed a reboot. The boot ID changed, the recovered kernel command line contained audit=1, auditctl reported enabled 1, and the persistent configuration still contained audit=1 after recovery.

requirements.requirement: Retain the installed RHEL release and kernel while using software compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: RHEL Server 7.9 and kernel 3.10.0-1160.el7.x86_64 were unchanged before and after the reboot. The executor used the already-installed RHEL 7 grubby/grub2 tooling and did not install or replace the operating system or kernel.

overall_summary: All material outcomes are satisfied. node1 rebooted onto audit=1, retained the setting in its boot configuration, recovered healthy under a new boot identity, and remained on the original RHEL 7.9 release and kernel.
limitations: Native package-manager consistency checks timed out both before and after execution, so package-database health could not be independently compared.

The two rollback backup files created during configuration were not included in the lifecycle inventories, so their final presence was not independently checked; their creation nevertheless had a clear recovery purpose.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. The configuration edits and rollback backups in cmd-d9986003bc6943b3 directly supported the required persistent boot change, while the scheduled reboot in cmd-a3e0a3eaa4cc45d5 was necessary to validate persistence and satisfy the restart-evidence protocol. Recovery showed no failed units or unexpected socket exposure; lifecycle temporary-file differences were normal systemd-private directories associated with the new boot. The restart protocol was complete: healthy pre-restart state and boot identity, acknowledged restart, different post-restart identity, active SSH, writable root filesystem, readable release data, and zero failed units, corroborated by fixed lifecycle observations.
